items.content:
Two critical PHP RCEs are patched: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS 9.2.
• Fixed in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

You can still focus on detection coverage today.

Security Labs writeup (coverage + guidance): https://t.co/aBB6g7gCZ5

Most PHP RCEs converge on the same outcome, whatever the bug: a web server process (php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2, httpd) doing something a request-serving daemon almost never does legitimately.

• a shell to confirm access: id, whoami, uname -a
• a second stage pulled in: curl http://... | bash
• a reverse shell: bash -i >& /dev/tcp//
• a webshell written into the web root

The bug class is public now: out-of-memory corruption, and stale state reused by the same worker. The behavior is what you detect.

We recently ran a different PHP RCE end-to-end (wp2shell): apache2 spawning dash to run id; whoami; hostname fired the exact rules that we suspect to catch php2shell. Payload Execution by Web Server kills the shell on the endpoint.

The Suspicious/Unusual Command, Child, and File Creation via Web Server rules stack on top.

(PHP did confirm partial php.ini mitigations. session.upload_progress.enabled=0 blocks the confirmed session paths only. Patch is still the fix.)

Patch to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Verify that the stack is enabled now.

Guidance + every rule link below.

items.content:
Let’s not forget about this certificate clusterfuck while everyone is busy with the PHP RCE news.

Almost at the same time, another serious security incident became public.

Eight intermediate CA certificates from eMudhra were found to use ridiculously weak private keys. We’re talking about P-384 keys where one private key was literally the number 4. FOUR!

Six of these were TLS CAs, allowing anyone to recover their private keys and potentially issue trusted certificates for arbitrary domains.

Major browsers have already blocked the affected CAs. But what about API clients, backend services, embedded devices, containers, and systems with outdated trust stores?

Many don’t enforce Certificate Transparency or check revocation. Some could remain vulnerable for years.

These weak keys have existed since April 2025. No confirmed malicious exploitation so far, but the implications are serious.

Don’t overlook this one while focusing on PHP.

items.content:
We had a Windows machine where one process kept coming back after every reboot.

At first, it looked like normal Windows activity because the service name was:

WindowsTelemetry

That sounds believable enough.

Windows has plenty of telemetry components, so if you are checking quickly, you might not even stop there.

But I checked the full service configuration.

The executable path was:

C:\Users\kevin\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Telemetry\telemetry.exe

That did not make sense.

A service running as LocalSystem should not normally be launching an unsigned executable from a user’s AppData folder.

I checked the file signature.

NotSigned

Then I checked when the service was installed.

Event ID 7045 in the System log showed that WindowsTelemetry had been created the previous night around 11:08 PM.

The service was configured to start automatically and run as LocalSystem.

That meant the binary was not just persistent.

It was running with very high privileges.

I pulled the PID for the service and checked its network activity.

The process had an established HTTPS connection to an external IP address.

At that point, we isolated the machine.

The interesting part for me was how normal the service looked from the name alone.

WindowsTelemetry

Microsoft\Telemetry

telemetry.exe

Everything was named to make you move past it.

But once you looked at the path, signature and service account, the picture changed completely.

This is why when I am reviewing Windows services, I do not only look for strange names.

I check what they actually execute.

I check where the file lives.

I check who signed it.

And I check which account the service runs under.

A malicious service does not need a suspicious name.

Sometimes it just needs a name boring enough that nobody bothers to open the properties.

items.content:
刚开始接触生物学的时候，我经常想象原始海洋里的有机分子构成核糖核酸，然后诞生了最早的单细胞生物，单细胞生物又聚在一起变成黏糊糊的原始多细胞生物，最终一步一步演化出各种生灵。我也经常想，如果能在实验室里加速重现这一过程，完整观察整个生物演化史就好了。

刚开始接触计算机的时候，我想过一个问题：程序是从哪里来的？后来我知道了编译器，程序从编译器来的。编译器自然也是从其它编译器来的。那么最早的编译器是从哪里来的？后来我逐渐搞清楚了这个问题的答案。但偶尔还是会想一些相关的问题，比如：如果现在全世界的编译器都忽然消失，人类要怎么重建整套体系呢？

最近几年研究 AI 安全问题的时候，我经常想：如果只给予 AI 完成特定工作所需的工具，那么 AI 的能力是不是就会被限制住？是不是就可以阻止 AI 获得强大的网络入侵能力？

2026 年 2 月，我看到马斯克预测到年底 AI 就可以绕过编译过程直接创建二进制文件。当时我做了一些实验，发现虽然 AI 还不能创建完整可运行的程序，但已经可以生成正确的机器码片段了。到了 9 月，我再次实验，发现此时 AI 已经可以用直接创建二进制文件的形式输出不太复杂的程序了。

但用直接输出二进制文件的方式去写大型程序显然不是好的选择，即使能写出来，也难以维护。那么，是不是可以让 AI 重演现代编译器的诞生过程？就像重演从核糖核酸到哺乳动物的生物演化史？

下面这个视频里超级马里奥游戏就是从核糖核酸开始构建的。

AI 先是通过直接输出二进制的方式构建了一个 3584 字节的机器码装配器 A0。然后用 A0 生产了一个更类似汇编器的工具 A1。又用 AI 生产了最基础的 C 编译器 C0。再一步一步迭代，最终演化出了一个完整支持 C89 标准并部分支持 C99 标准的编译器。有了这个编译器，就可以写出超级马里奥游戏，或者是任何网络攻击程序。

对 AI 说：“要有光”，然后整个世界就一步一步诞生了。所以我把这个项目命名为 BitKindle。感兴趣可以测试一下：https://t.co/GN9onM4vTq

items.content:
RT @andriinb: An enterprise environment emits billions of log events every day. During an incident, the responder rarely needs all of them. They need the few hundred or thousands that tell the story: the burst of 4625 failures followed by a single 4624 success, the encoded PowerShell spawned by winword.exe, the new service installed at 03:12 on a domain controller. Logs analysis is the discipline of getting from the first number to the second fast enough to matter.

That job has become harder in two directions at once. Attackers using AI tooling generate evidence at machine speed and pad real actions with benign-looking activity. Meanwhile, the obvious shortcut of pushing logs into an LLM runs into guardrails, context-window limits and data-protection obligations. Hugging Face’s responders hit exactly that wall in July 2026, when roughly 17,000 , later to be claimed 3 billion events (still healthy daily workload) were refused by frontier models and had to be processed on a local model instead.

Below, we cover log analysis end to end, then look at LogTotal, SOC Prime’s free answer to the incident-time version of the problem. https://t.co/wZaxcJwecZ

items.content:
My concern with the upcoming PHP RCE disclosure is how many systems could remain exposed long after patches become available.

Roughly a third of PHP websites still run PHP 5 or 7. Some operators will need to migrate old applications before they can move to a supported release. Even on supported versions, plenty of systems won't be patched immediately. Some owners won't notice the advisory; others can't deploy an update that quickly.

We still need the technical details to understand the actual exposure. If reliable, unauthenticated exploitation works across common deployments, I'd expect automated mass exploitation very quickly. AI-assisted exploit development and payload adaptation could shorten the response window further.

For detection teams, I'd prepare now for the activity that follows. I expect plenty of familiar shells, downloaders, webshells and persistence mechanisms, even though the entry point is new.

I've published a process-watcher guide with PHP configurations to record descendant processes and their command lines, with optional termination rules for shells, interpreters and known payload patterns:

https://t.co/7nluFV3Q25

Short-lived commands can still be recorded, even when they finish before the kill response arrives. Activity entirely inside the PHP worker remains a blind spot.

THOR Lite already includes relevant detections. We'll also review internally what additional post-exploitation coverage we can make publicly available.

After patching, check for compromise. An update doesn't remove an existing webshell or invalidate stolen credentials.
